faq.q: Why are macrolides preferred for atypical pneumonia?

exam: A 22‑year‑old student presents with 5‑day dry cough, low‑grade fever and normal chest X‑ray. What is your next step? — Start empirical macrolide therapy based on clinical syndrome.
How does Legionella pneumonia differ clinically from Mycoplasma pneumonia? — GI symptoms, hyponatraemia and higher severity suggest Legionella.
A pregnant woman with atypical pneumonia cannot tolerate oral meds. What is the safest IV option? — IV azithromycin, safe in pregnancy and effective against atypicals.
Why would you avoid a fluoroquinolone in a young adult with atypical pneumonia? — Risk of tendon rupture and cartilage toxicity; reserve for macrolide failure or severe disease.
What bedside sign helps distinguish atypical from typical pneumonia? — Absence of lobar consolidation on auscultation and diffuse crackles.

In a resource‑limited clinic without radiology, how do you decide to treat for atypical pneumonia? — Rely on history of gradual onset, dry cough, low fever, and epidemiologic clues; start macrolide empirically.

A patient with HIV presents with fever, cough and hyponatraemia. Which atypical pathogen is most likely and what is the preferred therapy? — Legionella; treat with macrolide (azithromycin) or fluoroquinolone if macrolide contraindicated.
What are red‑flag features that require urgent referral in a patient with suspected atypical pneumonia? — Respiratory distress, hypoxia, hypotension, altered mental status.
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Atypical pneumonia is caused by intracellular bacteria and requires macrolides as first‑line therapy. In low‑resource settings, clinical clues guide diagnosis and treatment when labs are limited.

b: Often milder than typical bacterial pneumonia
Chest X‑ray shows patchy infiltrates, not lobar consolidation
Community‑acquired, affects young adults and school‑aged children
sections.p: Atypical pneumonia presents with a sub‑acute cough, low‑grade fever and diffuse infiltrates. Common agents are Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae and Legionella spp.

b: History of gradual onset, dry cough, headache, myalgia
Physical exam: scattered crackles, no pleural rub
Serology or PCR if available; otherwise treat empirically
sections.p: Diagnosis relies on history, exam and limited investigations; macrolides are chosen for intracellular activity and safety in pregnancy.

b: Reduces risk of progression to severe pneumonia
Limits secondary bacterial infection
Important in HIV‑positive patients where atypical pathogens are common
sections.p: Prompt macrolide therapy reduces duration, prevents complications and limits spread in crowded settings such as schools and refugee camps.

t.b: Is there infiltrate pattern typical of atypical pneumonia? → Diffuse or interstitial infiltrates support diagnosis; normal film does not exclude it.

t.a: Rapid antigen test for Legionella (if available)
t.b: Detects Legionella spp.; positive result directs therapy toward macrolide or fluoroquinolone.
Leukocytosis mild or absent; lymphocytosis may suggest atypical cause.
Rely on clinical syndrome and start macrolide empirically.

b: Azithromycin or clarithromycin – chosen for intracellular penetration and safety in pregnancy
Avoid beta‑lactams alone – ineffective against intracellular organisms
If severe or contraindication to macrolide, use doxycycline (if not pregnant) or a respiratory fluoroquinolone
Hydration, antipyretics, and oxygen if SpO2 < 92 % on room air
sections.p: Treat the pathogen with a macrolide, provide supportive care, and monitor for deterioration.

b: Typical pneumonia: lobar consolidation, high fever, productive sputum, responds to beta‑lactams
Viral URI: normal chest X‑ray, prominent upper‑airway symptoms, no response to macrolides
sections.p: Typical bacterial pneumonia and viral upper respiratory infection.

Leukopenia can occur in severe Legionella infection
sections.p: Normal chest X‑ray early in disease and mild leukocytosis may falsely suggest a viral infection.

Check for extrapulmonary Legionella signs (GI symptoms, hyponatraemia)
Remember macrolides are safe in pregnancy – key for obstetric exam stations
sections.p: Focus on pattern recognition, empirical treatment, and safety of macrolides in pregnancy and HIV.
